2009 contraction in global IP was the worst since 1975, with only the strength of China preventing it from being the worst on record. Particularly hard hit were the investment sensitive areas of capital goods and autos production. Road to recovery will be prolonged, with activity in many economies taking years to get back to pre-crisis levels. China will continue to be the driving force in global industrial output. However, the need for rebalancing and the less favourable global conditions will result in a slightly slower pace of Chinese growth than during the period 2003 - 2007 Source: Datastream, Wood MacKenzie **www.woodmac.com** # **Copper Mine Disruptions – less of an impact moving forward?** Overall net loss in 2009 was the lowest in over five years at just 3.3% (545kt Cu) 2009 disruption losses were -4.8%, closures -2.2% offset by higher than expected output gains +3.7% Better than expected performances from mines such as PTFI, Chuqui, Escondida, Tenke and Prominent Hill Lower disruptions and more outperforming mines could indicate that the various supply constraints identified in recent years are becoming less of an issue 4.0%

## **www.woodmac.com** # **Main Risks to Short-Term Forecasts** ## **Lost mine output due to disruptions was far less in 2009 than in previous years** - Annual generic disruption forecast from 6% to 5% moving forward - Too early to tell whether this is too little (or indeed too much) - A 1% change in the disruption allowance is equivalent to 170kt Cu ## **Scrap remains an extremely important component of the overall copper supply/demand equation** - Difficult to monitor and forecast due to the highly fragmented/secretive nature of this market - Scrap growth will be constrained by moderate rise in industrial end-use activity in the developed economies - After declining by 15% in 2009 we expect overall scrap growth of ~5% in 2010, ~9% in 2011 and ~7% in 2012 ## **A repeat of the dramatic growth in investment fund activity in 2010 looks unlikely** - Sharply lower

commodity prices at the start of 2009 provided ideal buying opportunity for funds 

- Commodity price gains in the short/medium term unlikely to match the rises seen in 2009 



- Financial sector under intense scrutiny – stricter regulations could hamper future fund investment in commodities 

- **Recovery in consumption growth within developed economies likely to be drawn out** 

- “Cash for clunkers” initiatives drawing to a close 

- Ongoing malaise within the construction sector 



## **All eyes (again ) on China….** 

- Refined consumption affected by many variables (SHFE/LME, scrap, tariffs/duties, credit & offshore demand) 

- 2009 Chinese copper stock rise extended well into the consumption chain (at least through semis) 

- Speculative stocks lower than first thought but still uncertainty as to the timing of their release 



## **Overall copper stocks have risen to “normal” levels now but are expected to decline in 2011** 

- Overall stock position should be supportive of fundamental prices 

- Market remains vulnerable to short-term effects of any major fund sell off 

- Average annual prices expected to remain above $3/lb in the medium term through to 2012
